tips.text: Croatian **bollards** are white with a black rectangle and red or white reflector. From the top, it is shaped like a triangle.
tips.note: Hungarian and Lithuanian bollards look similar**, **but have more **rounded **edges compared to Croatia’s sharper edges. Lithuanian bollards will also have an orange reflector. North Macedonia sometimes uses similar bollards.

tips.text: Croatia features chevrons with a **red **arrow** **on a **yellow **or **white **background.
Croatia has **square (B-type) guardrails**.
tips.note: Croatia is one of the few European countries that use B-type guardrails. For a good overview of European guardrails, see [this infographic.](/images/croatia/europeguardrail.png)

tips.text: Generation 3 coverage often has a non-standard car blur where the **side mirrors** of the car are partially visible. This is not unique to Croatia, but by far most common there.
tips.note: Sometimes, you can see a small circular [**yellow **sticker](https://goo.gl/maps/8T97sBibVM3pgwEZ9) on the car mirror. This sticker is unique to Croatia.

tips.text:
Another quirk of Generation 3 coverage is that the majority of it was made in **autumn**. This means that the vegetation in this coverage will often have distinct yellowish or orange fall colours.

Take note that this seasonal meta is not found in Generation 4 coverage.
A black generation 4 car that will never have an antenna can be found in Croatia.
tips.note: A black car can be found in many European countries, though it will often have an antenna visible.

tips.text: A white generation 4 car that will never have an antenna can be found in Croatia.
tips.note: A white car can be found in many European countries, though it will often have an antenna visible.

tips.text: Stickers with the letters **HR **can be found on Croatian cars. HR stands for Hrvatska, the Croatian name for Croatia.
tips.note: These were mainly used before EU plates were introduced, meaning they will be less common in Generation 4.

tips.text: Croatia has direction signs with a **yellow background** and a **black **outline. They often have a pencil-shaped tip.
tips.note: The other former Yugoslav countries of Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro and North Macedonia have similar signs. A comparison can be seen [here](/images/croatia/croatia_directionsigncomp.png).

tips.text: Croatian utility poles are cylindrical and made of concrete or wood, often with **alternating hooks **on the [wooden poles](https://goo.gl/maps/tudAitHkDfNSgbQu5) (somewhat similar to Latvian poles).
Buildings in Croatia sometimes feature exposed **red brick walls**. This architecture is more common in inland areas.
tips.note: This type of architecture can also be found in Slovenia and Serbia.

tips.text: Croatia features **blue **fire hydrants with two diagonal protrusions on either side. Newer fire hydrants seen in Generation 4 have a [smaller top](https://www.google.com/maps/@45.3444374,19.0031362,3a,15y,342.71h,79.67t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sPvq5ffNHeVxmDooenAuoyA!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) but are still recognisable due to the blue paint.
tips.note: Similar fire hydrants can be found in bordering countries, most commonly in Hungary.

tips.text: Croatia’s pedestrian sign features a **pedestrian with a belt** and a zebra path with 5 stripes.
tips.note: The pedestrian on Slovenia’s sign does not have a belt.

tips.text:
**Karlovačko **and **Ožujsko** are common Croatian beer companies, with advertisements seen around the country.

**Konzum** and **Plodine** are common supermarket chains, mostly found in big cities. Plodine is exclusive to Croatia, while Konzum also operates stores in Bosnia.
Croatia does not have Generation 2 car coverage. However, in some historic downtown areas, a **Generation 2 trekker** camera was used.
tips.note: In some of this trekker coverage, the Google employee’s red cap is visible.

tips.text: The north-eastern region of Croatia is mostly **flat **and features a lot of agriculture. It is similar in terms of landscape to Hungary and north-western Serbia.
The region north and west of Zagreb is **hilly **and **agricultural**.

The Adriatic coast features **rocky **mountains similar to those seen in Montenegro or Albania. Shrubs are more common instead of trees along the coast, especially in the south. This coastal region has a lot of islands and peninsulas.
Houses and walls made of **beige brick** are common on the Adriatic coast. They often feature **green **shutters.
tips.note: Similar architecture can also be found in some regions in Italy. Additionally, Croatian shutters can also be white, beige etc.

tips.text: The north-western region of Istria, south of the Italian city of Trieste, sometimes has distinct **red **soil.
Bilingual street name signs with Croatian and **Italian** are typically found in Istria, especially in the western cities.
Town names ending with “**-ec**” are common to see in the northern parts of central Croatia.

Croatia’s capital Zagreb has a distinct **big city feel**. Apartment** **blocks can be seen throughout the city. The northern part of the city is hilly. Furthermore, Zagreb has [blue electric trams](https://goo.gl/maps/HKezsyENV7j4TJ1J7).
tips.note: In addition to regular car coverage, Zagreb also has various urban [sidewalk trekkers](https://goo.gl/maps/55CGuPvKbjzGLv4XA), often made with a Generation 2 camera.

tips.text: Zagreb and Osijek are the only two cities in Croatia with **trams**.
The region northeast of Zadar is recognizable as it is flat with a **mountain **ridge visible in the distance north.

There are a lot of vineyards around the town of **Ilok**, near the Serbian **border**,** **west of Novi Sad. You can find vineyards in other parts of Croatia as well, but they are most common in this area. If you see lots of vineyards in a northeastern Croatian landscape, you are more often than not near Ilok.
Traffic lights in Rijeka are held up by **long blue poles** that extend out over the road. These are exclusive to the city.
The town of Petrinja was severely damaged by an earthquake in 2020. As a result, many buildings can be seen **ruined** and undergoing repair.
The city of Dubrovnik in the far south of coastal Croatia is famous for its beautifully preserved **medieval city walls**, which can be seen from many points in and around the Old Town.
These tall **cypress trees** are commonly found near the southern tip of Croatia.
